newsitem.title: USA: Analysts still confident Fed will do coupon pass.
newsitem.headline: Analysts still confident Fed will do coupon pass.

text.p: Despite the U.S. Treasury market's growing frustration over the lack of a coupon pass during the last several weeks, analysts remain confident the Fed will buy coupons in the very near future.

Wednesday's afternoon selloff of about a half-point was attributed mostly to disappointment that the Fed did not buy coupons. Traders said that "day-traders" speculated the Fed would make its permanent, seasonal reserve add to the banking system by Wednesday. When that didn't happen, selling ensued.
Subsequently, there has been talk that the Fed won't add permanent reserves this year.

Analysts forecast the Fed's average daily add need at about $8 billion in the period beginning on Thursday, before jumping to about $12 billion in the following two-week period. The add need always jumps this time of year due to consumers' need for money for food, gifts and travel during the holiday season.

"The Fed needs to add permanent reserves; the question is when?" said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "I don't think they have a choice. We all make errors (in forecasting reserve needs), but with an add job this big, it seems hard to imagine that the Fed will address it (just through) daily open market operations."

The market has been looking for a coupon pass for two weeks. Some had figured the Fed would do one before Thanksgiving, since the holiday fell later in the month than usual. But when that failed to occur, the market set its sights on a coupon pass this week.
The Fed has bought coupons after Thanksgiving in six of the last eight years, analysts pointed out.
"Nothing is saying that they can't come in (on Thursday)," said UBS Securities money market analyst Kathy Bostjancic, who strongly believes that the Fed will soon buy coupons.

Analysts noted that since the Fed changed the way it does coupon passes two years ago, it bought coupons three times. Once, they started their multi-day tranche on a Wednesday. The other two times the coupon passes began on a Thursday and a Friday. Typically, the Fed buys a total of about $4.0 billion to $4.5 billion in coupons.
"It's arbitrary (as to) time and date and (at) which part of they curve they buy," Bostjancic said.

James Blumenthal, money market economist at MCM MoneyWatch, said it is possible the Fed won't buy coupons this year, but that scenario is very unlikely. "Maybe they have a different add need forecast for December," he said.
He also said rumored Fed purchases of coupons from foreign central banks over the past few trading sessions would largely accomplish the same purpose as buying coupons in the open market.
"I am still looking for (a coupon pass) but I wonder why they are waiting so long," Blumenthal said.
Dean Witter's Flanagan said he expects the Fed to do a coupon pass either Thursday, Friday or early next week.
"I tend to caution the market not to overreact here," he said. "It doesn't seem as if the Fed has much leeway."
Bostjancic added that it might be wise to wait for Thursday afternoon's reserve data before throwing in the towel.
"Each day (that the Fed doesn't buy coupons) diminishes the possibilty," she said. "But it doesn't reduce it to zero."
